subject.title: from Hero and Leander: "It lies not in our power to love or hate"
subject.author: Christopher Marlowe
subject.text:
It lies not in our power to love or hate,
For will in us is overruled by fate.
When two are stripped, long ere the course begin,
We wish that one should lose, the other win;
And one especially do we affect
Of two gold ingots, like in each respect:
The reason no man knows; let it suffice
What we behold is censured by our eyes.
Where both deliberate, the love is slight:
Who ever loved, that loved not at first sight?

title: The Least Romantic Line Ever Written About Love at First Sight
standfirst: Shakespeare thought enough of this couplet to quote it by name in one of his own plays. Read where it actually sits — after a warning word, a wrestling match and two identical bars of gold — and it argues something far less comforting than love at first sight usually gets credit for.

sections.heading: One Word Before the Line Everyone Keeps
sections.body: Hero and Leander see each other for the first time at a feast for Adonis in Sestos, and Marlowe's narrator plants a single word in the sentence that does it: they meet "where unhappily, / As after chanc'd, they did each other spy." Two lines later Love's arrow lands, Leander stands "stone still," and Hero's heart is "strook" by the look on his face. Then the narrator stops telling the story and starts arguing a case. That case ends in the ten lines everyone still quotes, closing with "Who ever lov'd, that lov'd not at first sight?" Read on its own, it sounds like a toast. Read straight after "unhappily," in a poem the two people in it don't survive, it sounds more like a diagnosis.

sections.heading: The Comparison Is Colder Than the Conclusion
sections.body: Before Marlowe reaches the line, he argues for it with two comparisons, and neither is romantic. First, spectators watching two men "stripp'd" for a race and picking a favourite "long ere the course begin," for no better reason than that someone has to lose. Second, the pull toward "one especially" of "two gold ingots like in each respect" — objects with no possible difference between them. "The reason no man knows," the narrator admits; "let it suffice, / What we behold is censur'd by our eyes." That is the argument the famous line closes out: love here is not fate finding its match, it is fate as blind favouritism, the same faculty that picks a side in a stranger's race. The scholar John N. Wall has argued the whole passage is built to be doubted rather than trusted, its confidence already undercut by the word "unhappily" two lines earlier.

sections.heading: A Short Greek Poem, Considerably Stretched
sections.body: Marlowe's chief source was not English, or even from his own century: a much shorter retelling of the same story by the Byzantine poet Musaeus Grammaticus. Nothing in a spare original obliges a poet to stop mid-scene and argue philosophy for ten lines before letting the lovers speak again — that habit belongs to Marlowe, and he repeats it through the whole poem, inflating a passing moment into a set piece and then moving on as if nothing had happened. The result is also, unfinished, an odd kind of monument: there is no Third Sestiad in Marlowe's own hand. His two sestiads break off at dawn, the morning after the couple's first night together, long before the story reaches the ending everyone already half-knows.

sections.heading: Registered to a Man Already Dead
sections.body: Whatever weeks or months Marlowe spent on the poem, they were his last. In spring 1593 he seems to have been staying at Scadbury, the Kent house of his patron Sir Thomas Walsingham, perhaps to sit out the plague; that same spring the informer Richard Baines handed the authorities a list of eighteen blasphemous statements he attributed to Marlowe, a warrant for his arrest went out on 18 May, and on 30 May he was killed in a house in Deptford — officially in a fight over the bill, though the coroner's account has long struck scholars as strange, and his killer was pardoned. Hero and Leander was entered in the Stationers' Register that September, four months after Marlowe was in the ground, credited to a man already dead. When Edward Blount finally published it in 1598, he dedicated the book to Walsingham with a line that reads like an apology for the five-year wait: he did not consider himself "discharged of the dutie wee owe to our friend, when wee haue brought the breathlesse bodie to the earth."

sections.heading: The Only Contemporary Shakespeare Ever Named
sections.body: Hero and Leander is, by the current count, the only work by a contemporary writer that Shakespeare quotes anywhere in his plays. In As You Like It, Phebe has just been dressed down by Ganymede for spurning the shepherd Silvius; the moment Ganymede leaves, she turns the line on herself: "Dead shepherd, now I find thy saw of might: / 'Who ever loved that loved not at first sight?'" "Dead shepherd" nods at Marlowe's own best-known shorter poem, The Passionate Shepherd to His Love, and at the plain fact that its author had been dead for years by the time the line was staged. What Phebe doesn't know, and the audience does, is that "Ganymede" is Rosalind in disguise — so Shakespeare's one direct homage to Marlowe lands in the mouth of a woman falling, at first sight, for another woman playing a man. Four centuries on, the line still gets quoted the way Phebe means it: sincerely, as a rule about the heart, with none of the wrestlers or gold ingots attached.

sections.heading: The Ending Marlowe Never Wrote
sections.body: Marlowe's own hand stops at dawn, the lovers still alive, still undiscovered. What happens next belongs to George Chapman, who finished the poem for print four sestiads later. A storm turns the Hellespont into a battle between winds; Hero tries to shield her signal-torch with her own robe as Leander swims toward it, and loses — "out, O, out it went!" Leander drowns within sight of her tower. When his battered body washes up, Hero climbs down, "fell on her love's bosom, hugg'd it fast, / And with Leander's name she breath'd her last." Neptune, moved to pity, turns the two of them into birds that "still in couples fly" — a small, strange mercy, granting in death the togetherness that the poem's opening argument said neither of them had ever really chosen. Whatever "unhappily" was warning about in that first temple scene, Chapman eventually got there.
